title: Identifying clinician perceived priorities for a real-time wearable system for in-hospital monitoring: findings and evolutions following the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: A Wearable Monitoring System (WMS), comprising a chest patch, wrist-worn pulse oximeter, and arm-worn blood pressure device, was developed in preparation for a pilot Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) on a UK surgical ward. The system was designed to support continuous physiological monitoring and early detection of deterioration.An initial prototype user interface was developed by the research team based on prior clinical experience and engineering knowledge. To ensure suitability for clinical practice, iterative user-centred refinement was undertaken through a series of clinician focus groups and wearability assessments. Six focus groups were conducted between November 2019 and May 2021 involving multidisciplinary healthcare professionals. Feedback from these sessions informed successive interface and system modifications.System development spanned the COVID-19 pandemic, during which the WMS was rapidly adapted and deployed to support clinical care on isolation wards. Feedback obtained during this period was incorporated into later versions of the system and provided a unique opportunity to examine changes in clinician priorities under pandemic conditions.Clinicians consistently prioritised alert visibility, alarm fatigue mitigation, parameter flexibility, and centralised monitoring. Notably, preferences regarding alert modality and access mechanisms evolved over time: early enthusiasm for mobile or smartphone-type devices shifted towards a preference for fixed, ward-based displays and audible alerts at the nurses’ station following pandemic deployment.Building on previous wearability testing in healthy volunteers, wearability testing using a validated questionnaire was completed by 169 patient participants during the RCT. The chest patch and pulse oximeter demonstrated high tolerability, whereas the blood pressure cuff showed poor wearability and was removed from the final system.These findings demonstrate the importance of iterative, clinician-led design for wearable WMS and highlight how extreme clinical contexts such as the COVID-19 pandemic can significantly reshape perceived requirements for safety-critical monitoring technologies.Competing Interest StatementThe authors have declared no competing interest.Funding StatementThis research was funded by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Oxford Biomedical Research Centre (BRC). output.evidence_of_randomization: The abstract mentions "a pilot Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT)" was planned, and wearability testing was "completed by 169 patient participants during the RCT." However, the manuscript itself reports on system development phases (focus groups, user-centred refinement, pandemic deployment feedback) and wearability assessment outcomes, not on the RCT intervention allocation or clinical outcomes.
output.reasoning: The manuscript analyzes empirical data from multiple phases including focus groups (n=6), wearability assessments in healthy volunteers, and wearability testing in 169 patient participants during an RCT. However, the primary focus is on system development, clinician preferences, and device tolerability rather than on evaluating health or clinical outcomes of a randomised intervention. While an RCT is mentioned as the context for the wearability assessment, the abstract does not report on the RCT's intervention allocation, randomisation method, or clinical outcomes. The data analyzed are primarily qualitative (clinician feedback) and device-focused (wearability ratings), not patient-level health outcomes. This appears to be a device development and usability study nested within an RCT, rather than a report of the RCT's clinical efficacy results.
